doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: John Hammond appears; the band never becomes solvent
summary: Carter showed Hammond around Harlem; the band looked promising but never solvent; the first day ends before Teddy Wilson.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Around this time John Hammond sort of comes into the picture. He was following the band and its formation, and was a big fan of yours and it. He began writing various pieces, particularly in the Melody Maker. Do you remember your first meeting up with John Hammond, or did he just start appearing around?
No, I don’t remember how we met, you know.
He said that you kind of took him in hand and showed him where things were happening uptown, which he . . .
Yeah, I showed him around Harlem.
. . . wasn’t aware of that much before that.
Yes.
That’s true, then.
I think so, yeah.
I guess as 1933 progressed, and you began to get some more work with this band, and it began to look like a more solvent kind of enterprise . . .
But it never became that. But go on.
But it looked like it. [laughs]
Yeah, yeah, it looked like it. You’re right. You’re right.
It had the potential, maybe.
Never became solvent, but go on.
You made a very important addition, and that was, of course, Teddy Wilson.
Teddy Wilson, yeah.
Can you go over that again, how that . . . [unclear], I guess, or hiring [unclear].
I think we’d better pick up on that tomorrow.
Okay. We will.
Yeah, I think we’d better call time.
